diagnostic_evidence.quote: the rescaling transformation can be explicited as $r_{n+1} = T(c_n,r_n)$

issues.failure_explanation: The outline asserts the paper shows the normalized roots are i.i.d. The paper proves only stationarity (each $r_n$ marginally uniform) and independence statements involving the scaling factors. Mutual independence of the roots is false: $r_{n+1}=T(c_n,r_n)$ with $T$ deterministic, so for the admissible deterministic cut $c\equiv 1/2$ (Section 2 allows any CDF $F$) the chain is the doubling map $r_{n+1}=2r_n \bmod 1$, and $r_{n+1}$ is a deterministic function of $r_n$; even with $\mathcal{U}(0,1)$ cuts, $\mathbb{P}[r_2<1/2\mid r_1=1/4]=3/4\neq 1/2$. Only the identical-marginal part holds.

failure_location.quote: we show that all the normalized roots are i.i.d., we explicitly describe the distribution of the scaling factor $\ell_n$

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Reword the outline to claim what is proved: the normalized roots are identically distributed (uniform from step 1 on), and under a uniform prior the scaling factors $\ell_i$ are i.i.d.; delete the claim that the roots themselves are independent.
issues.overall_effect: The introduction's summary of the paper's results asserts a false independence property of the root chain; no labelled result depends on it, but the prose misdescribes what is established.
issues.title: Outline overclaims that the normalized roots are i.i.d.
issues.why_classification: A one-sentence correction of an introductory summary; every formal result, rate and guarantee is unaffected.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: This shows that $r_{n+1}$ and $\ell_{n+1}$ are independent for all $n>0$.
Since the $\ell_i$ ($i>0$) are all independent, it follows that

issues.failure_explanation: Claim (ii) needs $(\ell_1,\dots,\ell_n)$ mutually independent. The proof's strong induction assumes that $r_n$ is independent of the vector $(\ell_1,\dots,\ell_n)$ and only derives that $\ell_{n+1}$ is independent of that vector; it never re-establishes the analogous joint statement for $r_{n+1}$ versus $(\ell_1,\dots,\ell_{n+1})$, which the next induction step requires. Pairwise statements (the only ones derived, via the one-step computation for $(r_1,\ell_1)$ repeated verbatim) do not give joint independence in general, so the induction never closes and (ii) is unproved as written.

failure_location.quote: Thus, $\ell_{n+1}$ is independent from $\ell_1,\dots,\ell_n$ for all $n>0$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Complete the induction with the joint invariant: prove by induction that $(r_n,c_n)$ is jointly independent of $(\ell_1,\dots,\ell_{n-1})$, that $r_n\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1)$ and $r_n\perp\ell_n$, using that $(r_{n+1},\ell_{n+1})$ is a deterministic function of the fresh pair $(r_n,c_n)$; this is a contained strengthening of the one-step computation already performed.
issues.overall_effect: Theorem thm - ind(ii) is unsupported as written; Corollary cor:added-2 ($\mathbb{E}[L_n]=\mathbb{E}[\ell_1]^n$), which uses mutual independence, and the conclusion's independence narrative lose their support.
issues.title: Independence of the scaling factors rests on an incomplete strong induction
issues.why_classification: The gap is filled by a routine strengthening of an argument the paper already carries out; the theorem's statement survives intact with no loss of guarantee, so the repair is contained.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: if $r_0$ does not have a point mass at $0$ or $1$ and if the cuts are not almost surely at 0 or 1, then
to note that the conditions in \Cref{thm - root_conv} are optimal

issues.failure_explanation: The hypotheses do not exclude root-cut ties of positive probability, and there the conclusion fails. Counterexample within the hypotheses: $r_0\equiv a$ and $c_n\equiv a$ for an interior $a$ (e.g. $a=1/2$, the deterministic bisection cut). Then $c_0=r_0$ a.s., and by the paper's own map $T(c,r)=r/c$ for $c\geq r$ the root jumps to $1$ and is absorbed ($T(c,1)=1$ for all $c<1$), so $G_k\to\delta_1\neq t$; Algorithm 2's tie rule (cut strictly above the root) instead rescales the root to $0$ — the two conventions disagree on ties, and neither converges to uniform. The proof breaks exactly at this point: the continuity step passes the limit $\lim_{t\to1}G(tc)=G(c)$, which needs left-continuity of $G$ at $F$-atoms (false at atoms of $G$), so $\mathcal{T}G_0$ (here the CDF of a point mass) leaves $B_\circ[0,1]$ and the Gavrea-Ivan theorem is invoked outside its hypotheses; likewise the identity for $\mathcal{T}G_n$ and the formula for $H_n$ silently drop the tie mass $\mathbb{P}[r_n=c_n]$.

failure_location.quote: If $r_0$ does not have a point mass at $0$ or $1$ (that is, $\mathbb{P}[r_0=0]=\mathbb{P}[r_0=1]=0$) and if the cuts $c_n$ are not almost surely at 0 or 1, then

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add a no-tie hypothesis (e.g. the cut distribution has no atoms; more generally $\mathbb{P}[c_n=r_n]=0$ for all $n$, which then propagates) and align the boundary conventions in the operator identity and in $H_n$ with it; under this hypothesis $G_n$ has no atoms at $F$-atoms, the dominated-convergence step is valid, the iterates stay in $B_\circ[0,1]$, and the Gavrea-Ivan argument applies unchanged, restoring the theorem and its dependents.
issues.overall_effect: The main general-prior uniform convergence theorem and its rate bound are false as stated for atomic priors paired with atomic cuts sharing an atom; the convergence claim of thm - pdf_general, the mean/variance limit cor - mean_variance_gen, the closing Remark's rates, and the 'optimal conditions' prose become unreliable.
issues.title: Convergence theorem fails for atomic priors paired with atomic cuts (root-cut ties)
issues.why_classification: The repair is one standard regularity condition plus a local patch of the atom bookkeeping; the advertised guarantee survives in full for every atomless cut law (the regime used in all experiments), only the degenerate atomic pairings — where the conclusion is provably false — are excluded, so nothing comparable is lost but more than a typo is needed.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: a random trisection method ($K=2$) with uniform cuts has, on average, the same scaling factor at each step as the deterministic bisection method, assuming the root is uniformly distributed.

issues.failure_explanation: By the paper's own formula $\mathbb{E}[\ell_n]=2/(K+2)$: at $K=2$ the factor is $1/2$, exactly the classical bisection factor (as the very next sentence says), and for $K\ge3$ the factor $2/(K+2)<1/2$ is better than classical bisection. The sentence therefore asserts the opposite of what is proved; the intended comparison is with the deterministic $(K+1)$-section factor $1/(K+1)$, which the random version roughly doubles.

failure_location.quote: the stochastic bisection method with $K$ cuts uniformly chosen has a factor of reduction which is approximately twice as bad as the classical bisection method

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Reword the sentence to compare with the deterministic $(K+1)$-section: the random factor $2/(K+2)$ is approximately twice $1/(K+1)$, with equality to classical bisection at $K=2$ as already stated in the next sentence.
issues.overall_effect: The section's efficiency comparison is materially misleading (the correct statement is the opposite for $K\ge2$); the formal results themselves are unaffected.
issues.title: Random multisection misdescribed as roughly twice as bad as classical bisection
issues.why_classification: A one-sentence local correction; every formal result and guarantee is preserved.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Draw $M=10000$ initial roots from the distribution $\mathcal{R}$;
Do a single step of \Cref{alg:bisection} with $c_n\sim \mathcal{U}(0,1)$ for each of the $M$ roots.
By contrast, the asymmetric distributions converge more slowly, at a rate closer to the upper bound given by the theorem.
with the initial $r$ drawn with respect to distribution $\mathcal{R}$. The initial root distribution is always $\mathcal{U}(0,1)$, so $\mu_{\ell_n}\to 2/3$.

issues.failure_explanation: In the described experiment the cuts are uniform and only the initial root follows $\mathcal{R}$; by the paper's own theorem the operator, hence the theoretical decay factor $1-2\,\mathbb{E}[c(1-c)]$, depends only on the cut distribution and equals $2/3$ for every $\mathcal{R}$. The 'Theoretical' row instead lists $1-2\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{R}}[c(1-c)]$ (0.6, 0.7714..., 0.9385..., 0.5083-overline{3}), i.e. the contraction factors obtained when those distributions are used for the CUTS — a benchmark no theorem provides for this experiment. The means experiment is additionally described inconsistently ('initial $r$ drawn with respect to $\mathcal{R}$' vs 'The initial root distribution is always $\mathcal{U}(0,1)$'); under the latter the means are exactly constant by Corollary cor - constant, so the reported nonzero decay rates could not arise. The claimed theory-experiment agreement ('at a rate closer to the upper bound given by the theorem') is therefore unsupported as written.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: State which quantity actually follows the distribution $\mathcal{R}$ in the experiment, make the descriptions consistent, and replace the 'Theoretical' row by the rate the theorems give for that setup (with uniform cuts: $2/3$ for every $\mathcal{R}$), or re-run the experiment with the setup the row presumes; revise the concluding comparison accordingly.
issues.overall_effect: The numerical validation of the convergence-rate theory for asymmetric priors (Figure ks_beta012, Table tab:convrate, and the concluding comparison) is unreliable: the theoretical benchmark does not follow from the proved results for the stated procedure, and the experimental setup is internally contradictory.
issues.title: Convergence-rate study benchmarks experiments against an inapplicable theoretical rate
issues.why_classification: Resolution requires re-specifying the experiment and recomputing or re-benchmarking the comparison, and it withdraws the claimed empirical match for asymmetric priors — contained, but more than a local typo; no formal theorem is lost.
